div.p: PART I: THE CONTINUATION AND FURTHER SPREAD OF THE WAR—EFFORTS TOWARD PEACE

p.hi: The Attitude of European Neutral States—Conditions in the Central Empires—Informal Discussion of Negotiations and Terms of Peace

row.cell: Effect of the war upon the internal affairs of Switzerland.
Transmits statement of Minister of Foreign Affairs regarding Sweden’s neutrality.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Reports a conversation with General French on war situation and peace proposal which he says the President has submitted to England at Germany’s request.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
German propaganda in the United States has aroused British suspicion of U. S. neutrality.
Scandinavian countries agree to act in unison and preserve neutrality.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Italy will probably go to war, if Turkey moves against Egypt.
Portugal virtually at war with Germany although war has not been declared.
Had good reason for sending cipher message of previous day.
Suggests that Colonel House will be of great help in peace plan.
Germany would be agreeable to peace proposals emanating from the Allies. Suggests that representatives be sent quietly to Allied countries with this in view.
Instructions to report in detail on military and economic condition of Germany.
Favorable moment for peace is passing with German victory over Russia. Asks that Colonel House bring peace proposals to Germany.
Report on military and economic condition of Germany.
Victory of the Germans over Russians in East Prussia complete.
Italy and Roumania will probably remain neutral; Bulgaria likely to join Germany; rumors that Japan will make separate peace and attack America; Germany winning; Allies must propose peace first.
Greek authorities are divided on war policy.
Von Jagow invites Colonel House to Berlin.
It is proposed that neutral powers address identical peace notes to the belligerents. Italy refuses.
Greece prepares to join the Allies_ _ _
The King opposes policy of the Prime Minister; latter resigns.
Austria is negotiating with Italy to gain her alliance.
Believes that Austria is attempting to purchase Italy’s non-entry into the war.
Discussion of Germany’s retention of Belgium: hatred against the United States is far-reaching.
Allies seeking support of Italy; Germany pressing for her continued neutrality.
Neither he nor British Ambassador thinks Italy and Austria will come to terms.
Further report on military and economic conditions in Germany.
Report of internal situation in Germany, hostile attitude toward the United States, and potential influences on the outcome of the war.
Semiofficial news article declares it America’s duty to restore peace.
Prominent Americans are en route to a peace conference at The Hague.
Asks that protection be given American women sailing on the Noordam for conference at The Hague.
Semiofficially stated that there will be no peace until object of the war is attained.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to arrange for safe passage of American delegates to the International Peace Congress.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Steamer Noordam has proceeded to Rotterdam.
Instructions to keep Department advised as to status of negotiations between Italy and Austria.
Rumors that Italy has declined Austria’s offer of the Trentino and has secured a loan in England.

p.hi: Italy’s Entrance into the War—The Diplomatic Contest in the Near East—Further Information Concerning the Central Empires—Private Efforts toward Peace

row.cell: Italy is reported to have signed agreement with the Allies guaranteeing to her territorial extension in exchange for military support.
Events point to Italy’s decision to join the Allies.
Is convinced that war between Austria and Italy is imminent. Will take charge of Austrian affairs provisionally.
Probability of immediate denunciation of treaty with Austria and Germany as first step towards war, which can only be obviated by Austria’s acceding to Italy’s demands.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Foreign editor of the Times states confidentially that the Allies have agreed to cede part of Austria to Italy if she comes into the war within a month.
Rumor of division in the Cabinet.
Giolitti’s antiwar policy seemingly predominates. Ministry has resigned.
Rumored that King has refused to accept resignation of Ministry.
It is believed that War Ministry will be reinstated and that war is probable.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria.
Triple Entente is working to secure alliance of Bulgaria; latter now more favorably inclined toward the Entente.
War feeling increasing, pointing to alliance with Triple Entente.
Vote for war in the Chamber and Senate almost certain.
Chamber of Deputies approves a defense program.
Senate confers full powers on the Government. War imminent.
Mobilization called and state of war declared in provinces on Austrian border and Adriatic.
Transmits Italy’s announcement of war with Austria-Hungary.
American Embassy is asked to take charge of Russian interests in Turkey in case of war between those countries.
Austrian and German Ambassadors have left Italy.
Transmits Italy’s justification for war against Austria-Hungary.
No declaration of war with Germany but German Embassy demanded passports.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Roumania ready to join Triple Entente if demands are granted. Bulgaria waiting for completion of contract agreed upon with Triple Entente. Typhus in Servia checked; credit given to Americans.
Prefers to decline care of Russian interests and act for Italy alone.
The President desires American Embassy to take over representation of Russia in Turkey to increase influence for peace.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Because of Russian reverses, Roumania may remain neutral.
Will represent Russian interests in Turkey, since it is part of the President’s plan.
Jane Addams reports on economic conditions and public opinion in Austria and Germany. Cooperation of the Pope in her peace movement is promised.
Gives views of the Russian Ambassador regarding German-American relations and predicts Italy’s declaration of war with Germany and Turkey.
Greece will probably enter the war. Allies still treating with Servia to cede part of Macedonia to Bulgaria.
Italy will give her subjects time to leave the Ottoman Empire before declaring, war on Turkey. Bulgaria may join the Allies if Italy sends forces to the Dardanelles.
Report on the points requested by the Department.
Ottoman Government yielded to ultimatum allowing Italians to depart. Interests of Italy, Russia, and Montenegro, except at Constantinople, are in his charge.
Germany has hope of capturing Russian Army; demarcation between parties favoring annexations and those opposing them, is plain.
Report on conditions in the Monarchy at the end of one year of warfare.

Peace appeal of the Pope received coldly because he fails to distinguish between those contending for the independence of nations and those showing contempt of right and principle. Poincaré demands a peace that will guarantee security of Europe.
Sets forth Italy’s grievances against the Turkish Government and reasons for declaration of war.
Transmits text of Chancellor’s speech before the Reichstag, Aug. 19, 1915, charging the Allies with responsibility for the war.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria.
If Bulgaria enters the war Roumania’s position between her and Austria-Hungary will be bad. Latter demands transit of ammunition through to Turkey.

p.hi: Bulgaria’s Entrance into the War—The Allies’ Intervention in Greece—Conditions in Russia and the Balkan States—Discussions in Various Countries of the Possibilities of Peace: Informal and Private Efforts

row.cell: Germany and Bulgaria have signed a military convention.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
It is believed that an agreement has been signed between Bulgaria and Turkey, and that German-Austrian army will attack Servia, in which case Roumania will join Servia.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
German influence and corruption of high officials cause reverses in Russia. Duma investigates expenditures for army supplies. Russia will make no separate peace.
Russia’s ultimatum to Bulgaria probably means hostilities. Allied forces expected in Saloniki.
To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Requests opinion on Balkan situation and frequent reports.
Italian Minister at Sofia and Bulgarian Minister at Rome requested to leave.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Russian ultimatum to Bulgaria and answer thereto.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Bulgaria has attacked Servia. Roumania will remain neutral. Rumored Greek Prime Minister, forced to resign because he failed to induce Roumania to join Greece in aid of Servia.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria.
Servia has decided to cede territory to Bulgaria; apprehensive of being overrun by German-Austrian armies en route to Turkey.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Has learned that Great Britain will consider no terms of peace that do not include the restoration of Belgium and northern France.
Reports indicate that Bulgaria has attacked Servia without declaring war.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Was informed on Oct. 15 of war between Great Britain and Bulgaria.
Transmits text of declaration of state of war between France and Bulgaria.
From the Third Assistant Secretary of State.
Reports official notice of a state of war between Italy and Bulgaria.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Bulgaria expects to gain more by joining the Central powers. Roumanian people for the Quadruple Entente, but King and higher powers favorable to Germany. Servia facing defeat.
Rumored that Von Bülow is making offers to Italy to withdraw from the war.
Minister of War sends message to the President that the time is opportune for peace negotiations.
Repeated rumor that Von Bülow is trying to associate the Pope with a league of neutral nations.
Germany and Bulgaria have raised question of neutrality of Greece if Servians, French, and English are driven back on Greek soil. French warn Greece against disarming Allied soldiers.
Peace conference is postponed because no French or English delegates can be secured.
Greece impressed by Allies’ suggestion of blockade and will remain neutral for the present.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria.

Roumania seeks to remain neutral; Central and Allied powers striving to gain her support. War loan will be made by Great Britain. Roumania refuses to permit Germany and Austria to transport ammunition through to Turkey.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria.
Speculations as to why Bulgaria joined the Central powers instead of the Allies.

Germany, on overrunning Servia, will make proposals of peace, demanding control of Belgium, Poland, and Servia. Bulgaria to be given territory in Macedonia. Italy asks cooperation of Allies in sending forces to Albania.
Mobilization of Greek army. Occupation of Saloniki by Anglo-French troops. Forces sent to Servia.
Italy has signed London agreement not to make separate peace; will aid Servian army. Greece has given assurance of conforming with her agreement.
Italy’s part in Albania considered to be sending of troops.
Department assumes no responsibility for activities of the Ford peace party.
To the Ambassadors and Ministers in all European Countries and Japan (telegram).
The Government is not concerned in the Ford peace movement.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria.
Discusses with officials the prospects of peace and the position Bulgaria will hold among the nations.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria.
Explains influences which decided Bulgaria in joining the Central powers.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria.
Defines Bulgaria’s attitude towards other Balkan states and relations with Turkey, including signing of protocol for the cession of Turkish territory.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Résumé of official memorandum showing neutrality policy of the Netherlands.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Austria and Germany arrange to buy wheat of Roumania.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Defeat of French and English troops in Macedonia causes Roumania to lean towards the Central powers.
To the Ambassadors in Great Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, and Russia (telegram).
Colonel House is sent by the Presiident to impart information to our ambassadors concerning the attitude of this Government and to obtain the points of view of the belligerents.
Switzerland will not propose peace until the belligerents desire it.
Ford peace party failed in its object.
Lorillard reports rupture of relations between Austria and Albania.
Ford peace party had no effect upon public opinion.
Following bomb dropping by German-Austrian aeroplanes, the British and French have seized the consulates of the Central powers and deported their consuls.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria.
Unofficially informed that the Central powers are satisfied with the territory gained in the war and are ready for peace.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria.
Discusses Bulgaria’s ambitions. Ultimate disposition of Servia is undecided.

p.hi: Proclamations, Orders, and Decrees of Belligerent Governments Affecting the Trade of Neutral States—Attitude of the United States and Other Neutral Governments

the german declaration of a naval war zone (february 4, 1915): position taken by the united states—negotiations relative to the admission of food supplies into germany—use of neutral flags by belligerent merchant vessels

row.cell: Germany warns merchant vessels of her intention to employ war measures against English transports and shipments of ammunition to France.
Germany declares a naval war zone and suggests a safe route for neutral shipping.
Italian Government asks the attitude of the United States regarding the German declaration of a naval war zone.
Position of the United States on naval war zone not yet determined.
Suggests U. S. representations to Great Britain regarding use of American flag by British merchant vessels.
German Government gives assurance that foodstuffs imported to Germany will be used by civilian population only.
Transmits copy of memorandum of the German Government of Feb. 4 concerning retaliation against Great Britain’s illegal interference with trade between neutrals and Germany.
From the Netherland Minister of Foreign Affairs to the Netherland Minister at Washington (telegram).
Netherland Government protests against the extent of the German war zone.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Foreign Office announces that use of neutral flag with limitations is an established ruse de guerre and that Germany has no right to destroy vessels and cargo before ascertaining their character.
Protest against proclamation of a war zone in waters surrounding Great Britain.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to call attention of the British Government to menace to Americans in use of American flag by British vessels.
The campaign of hate against America will be increased if the Department takes no action against the use of American flag by the Lusitania.
Scandinavian countries will send a joint note to Germany protesting against extent of war zone, also a note to Great Britain protesting against use of neutral flag by British vessels.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain
Grey will reply to telegram of Feb. 10 after conferring with Cabinet and Admiralty.
German proclamation will be withdrawn if England will adopt Declaration of London or allow food for civil population to enter Germany.
Statement of the German Government regarding plan for supplying the civil population with foodstuffs.
Campaign of hate against America approved by Government. American ships to be destroyed without investigation.
Germany may propose that American merchant vessels be convoyed by warships.
Germans claim Americans are partial to England and are supplying Allies with ammunition.
The new German method of naval warfare is justified. Describes British naval policy.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Protests against placing American steamer Wilhelmina in British prize court.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
German Government is willing that foodstuffs sent to Germany be distributed by American organizations to civil population.

German assurances regarding foodstuffs for civil population have been communicated to Great Britain, and respresentations made for release of
Wilhelmina.
Colonel House is commissioned to act in matters where several governments are involved. Instructions to act only upon his advice.
Comment of Minister for Foreign Affairs upon U. S. note to Germany regarding use of neutral flag by belligerents.
Swedish notes of protest sent to England and Germany regarding neutral shipping; Norway and Denmark to file identical notes.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Could Netherlands count on moral support of United States if a Dutch ship is sunk by Germans under naval declaration of Feb. 4?
Instructions to keep Department advised as to situation.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
The Netherlands may count on sympathetic attitude of the United States in shipping difficulties
Unofficial suggestions for neutral shipping in British waters.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British may propose not putting food on contraband list if Germany will refrain from submarine war on commerce. Offensive language of Bernstorff’s note a hindrance to agreement.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to urge admission into Germany of food for non-combatants in exchange for concessions equally important to be made by Germany.
Transmits reply to U. S. protest against war zone in waters surrounding Great Britain.
Germany willing to grant River Tyne as port free of mines and submarines for neutral vessels which guarantee not to carry contraband.
If England permits foodstuffs and raw material to enter Germany proposed blockade will be withdrawn. Otherwise safe routes around north of Scotland under convoy of war vessels can be arranged.
Regarding the Wilhelmina. Germany’s submarine warfare was begun before England’s interference with food for Germany.
Italy has informed Germany that she can not tolerate any restrictions on high seas except in accordance with international law. She suggests concerted action on part of neutrals.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits Grey’s justification for action of Lusitania and use of neutral flag.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
No hope of agreement between Germany and England regarding blockade and food.

p.hi: proposals of the united states for an agreement between the belligerents restricting the use of mines, submarines, and neutral flags and for the admission of foodstuffs into germany (february 20, 1915)

row.cell: To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). The same to the Ambassador in Germany.
Suggestions as basis for an agreement that will relieve neutral shipping.
Admiralty requests information as to sailing of American ships in order to safeguard their passage.
German Admiralty is resolved to starve England; the Government considers America unjust.
From the Netherland Minister of Foreign Affairs to the Netherland Minister at Washington (telegram).
Inquiry and comment concerning reservation of River Tyne for traffic of neutral vessels.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
U. S. suggestions of agreement between Germany and England regarding neutral shipping submitted to Allies.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Netherland Government states that British Admiralty furnishes arms to merchant vessels. Requests confirmation of this.
Department conferring daily with representatives of neutrals on subject of concerted action.
Germany inclined to accept proposed basis for an agreement with Great Britain under certain conditions.
Transmits copies of Italian memoranda: one to Germany protesting methods of maritime warfare and one to Great Britain protesting the use of Italian flag by British ships.
Instructions to report upon truth of statement regarding Germany’s assurance of respect for Italian flag.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Grey states that British policy regarding food for Germany is the consequence and not the cause of Germany’s practice of torpedoing merchant ships.
Sweden is discussing with Great Britain questions of convoy, neutral zone, or neutral port to aid neutral snipping.
Suggests that distribution of foodstuffs in Germany be superintended by committee not connected with the Government. If England objects, suggests that America place embargo on export of arms.
Regarding the agreement with England, Germany asks passage not only for food but for raw material.
Von Jagow states Germany has given instructions to respect bonafide neutral flags.

p.hi: the british and french declaration prohibiting all trade with germany (march 1, 1915)—orders and decrees for its enforcement protests of the united states proclamations concerning contraband of war replies to the proposals and protests of the united states

row.cell: Germany’s opponents driven to retaliatory measures regarding commodities, but they will be enforced without risk to neutral or non-combatant life.
From the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to the British Ambassador at Washington (telegram).
U. S. proposal to restrict use of submarines in exchange for permission for food to enter Germany is under consideration.
Diplomatic opinion regarding latest U. S. proposal.
Department cannot accept suggestion regarding embargo on munitions from America if England refuses food to Germany.
Admiralty declares the extent of war area and requests that English, Japanese, and Servian Governments be notified.
From the Ambassador in Germany (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits German reply to U. S. suggestion that certain principles be agreed upon by Germany and England in maritime warfare.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Suggests unity of action by United States and other neutrals to protect their citizens and commerce.
Emperor bitter against America. Military and naval heads have made terms of agreement with England impossible.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). Similar telegram to the Ambassador in France.
Proposed method of blockade of German ports unknown to international law; gives neutrals no standard by which to measure rights or avoid danger.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
American efforts for peace unappreciated in England.
From the Netherland Minister to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Transmits text of Netherland note to Great Britain protesting against the abuse of neutral flags and of note to Germany protesting the war-zone declaration.
Transmits list of lubricating oils to be treated as conditional contraband.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
No evidence that British have ordered transatlantic merchantmen to arm; and no arming prior to German submarine “blockade”.
German Government attempting to stir up hatred for America.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Proclamation of Mar. 11 makes additions to lists of contraband.
Transmits copies of Swedish notes to Germany and Great Britain protesting against conditions of neutral shipping and misuse of neutral flags.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits Grey’s reply of Mar. 13 to U. S. note suggesting terms of agreement with Germany as to conduct of the war at sea.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits order in council of Mar. 11, and note from Grey regarding restriction of German trade.
Transmits French reply to U. S. note regarding restriction of German trade.
Scandinavian countries have sent notes to Great Britain and France protesting against interruption of trade.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
New methods of warfare have changed the definition of blockade. German submarine blockade is failure; provoked English blockade of Germany, which is effective.
Transmits copies of Russian prize laws with recent modifications.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Public opinion looks to the United States for leadership in maintaining neutral rights.
From the Netherland Foreign Office to the Netherland Legation at Washington (telegram).
Netherlands takes exception to encroachment upon neutral rights by Allies.
Encloses decree of Mar. 13, 1915, regarding treatment of shipping bound to or from German ports
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Protests Allies’ methods of warfare and maintains rights of neutrals under rules of international law.
Reply to Great Britain protesting against restriction of trade with Germany.
Transmits memorandum on German-American trade and the question of delivery of arms to Allies.
Transmits copy of identic note from Norway to France and Great Britain protesting their war measures.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Press comment on U. S. note is friendly and shows appreciation of American position.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Inquires whether British merchant vessels have armed to resist submarines.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Proposes that the United States cooperate with the Netherlands in protecting their trade.
Defines lubricants and notes transfer of articles to list of absolute contraband.
Statement of position of the United States in maintaining its neutrality.
Submits for approval of United States a list of contraband in revision of treaty of 1871.
United States will raise no question as to list of contraband proposed by the Italian Government.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Additions and amendments to list of contraband.

p.hi: blockades in the mediterranean area—the british argument for the blockade of germany—further extensions of contraband lists

row.cell: Transmits Italian declaration of blockade of Austro-Hungarian and Albanian coasts.
Transmits Italian note defining the limits of the Albanian blockade.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits British note proclaiming blockade of the Asia Minor coast including the Dardanelles.
Transmits Italian note extending blockade of the Adriatic.
Transmits Italian contraband list and statement of principles to be applied by Italy in the war.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits note from Grey in answer to American criticism of blockade.
Protests against Italian restrictions of neutral rights on coasts of Albania and the Adriatic.
Gallipoli designated as convenient place for visit and search. Assurances of safety to American shipping.
Transmits Italian note giving further explanations of blockade and assurances of consideration for neutrals.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Encloses proclamation placing cotton and its products on absolute contraband list.
France has declared blockade of coast of Asia Minor and Syria.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits revised contraband list of Oct. 14, 1915.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits British note declaring blockade of Bulgarian coast on the Aegean.
Protests against blockade of neutral shores on Adriatic.

p.hi: the annulment by great britain and france of article 57 of the declaration of london

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits order in council of Oct. 20, 1915, annulling Art. 57 of the Declaration of London.
From the Vice Consul at London (telegram).
Subsequent to abrogation of Art. 57, nationality of a prize is to be determined by prize court.
Encloses copy of French report showing difficulties in application of Art. 57 of Declaration of London, and decree of Oct. 23, 1915, modifying it.
From the Vice Consul at London.
Parliamentary discussion of abrogation of Art. 57 of Declaration of London.

p.hi: Correspondence and Informal Arrangements Regarding the Exportation to European Countries of Various Particular Commodities Affected by the Proclamations, Orders, and Decrees of Belligerent Governments on Contraband of War and Trade with Enemy Countries
shipments of copper

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British Government offered to buy whole output of copper from America during the war, but producers refused.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Department not in position to object to classification of copper as contraband; quotes authorities regarding “continuous voyage.”
Asks aid of Department in securing British Admiralty certificate to ship copper.
Arrangement for special shipments of copper can be made with the British Admiralty.
British demand that American copper for Norway must be shipped on British vessels via Great Britain.

p.hi: shipments of cotton

row.cell: Inquires if cotton may be shipped to Germany.
England and France give assurances that cotton will not be seized.
Inquiry regarding linters for shipment to Austria.
Linters for manufacture of ammunition would probably be held contraband.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
American Ambassador, London, telegraphs that cottonseed oil may be shipped without hindrance.
To the Consul General at London (telegram).
Instructions to inquire if cotton yarn is non-contraband.
From the Consul General at London (telegram).
Asks if cotton linters may be shipped as non-contraband.
Cotton linters for manufacture of ammunition may be considered contraband.
To the Consul General at London (telegram).
Asks if cotton linters are considered contraband.
From the Consul General at London (telegram).
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits request from Spring Rice to Grey that cotton owners be permitted to fill German orders contracted for prior to issuance of contraband declaration.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to ask British Government for exemption for vessels and cotton cargoes under charter contracted for prior to Mar. 1.
Public announcement by the British Embassy.
Arrangement made for shipment of cotton contracted for prior to Mar. 2.
From the Consul General at London.
Possibility that cotton will be placed on contraband list; matter again being discussed.
From the Consul General at London.
Blockade measures seem to make special action on cotton unnecessary.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Cotton arrangements between British Government and Americans have no official connection with our Government.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British understand that cotton arrangement does not involve our Government nor affect the American attitude towards the order in council.
From the Augusta Cotton Exchange and Board of Trade (telegram).
Resolution protesting the confiscation by England of cotton shipped to neutral countries.
Urges measures for prompt relief of cotton market.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Increasing agitation regarding cotton as contraband.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Cotton will be declared contraband and England will offer to buy large quantities.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Allies discussing question of cotton with view to declaring it contraband.
Wood cellulose substituted for cotton in making munitions. Germany ready to assure that cotton will be used solely for civilians.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to take up with British the subject of cotton shipments to neutral European countries.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Arrangements with the British Government to send American cotton to Swedish Cotton Spinners Association.

p.hi: shipments of fruit

row.cell: From the Consul General at London (telegram).
American fruit must be consigned to Netherlands Oversea Trust; not so with southern fruits.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Instructions to protest if discrimination is shown against American fruit.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
The Netherlands makes no discrimination in receiving fruit.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Restriction against American fruit appears unjust.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British allow certain goods to enter Holland in exchange for special concessions; would probably cooperate with United States in same way.
Requests Department to arrange for shipments of apples to Holland. Tobacco on free list.
Fruit may be consigned to Oversea Trust. Agreement between Great Britain and Holland explained.

p.hi: shipments of naval stores

row.cell: To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Asks definition of “resinous substances” and on what grounds they are ranked as contraband.
Emphasizes importance of the rosin trade in the south.
Rosin shipped prior to declaration may be seized but must be paid for.
Explains attitude of the British Government on shipments of rosin.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Instructions to request the British Government to remove rosin from contraband list.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits British note setting forth reason for declaring resinous products contraband.

p.hi: shipments of tobacco

row.cell: To the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Quotes messages from the American Minister at The Hague regarding discrimination in tobacco trade; forwards U. S. views for presentation to British Government.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits British note in reply to representations regarding discrimination in tobacco trade.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Sets forth complaints of tobacco exporters. The United States expects American tobacco to be accorded same privileges as other tobacco.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Instructions to urge Foreign Office to allow shipments of tobacco to neutrals Without proof that it will not reach Germany.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British agree not to interfere with tobacco shipped to neutral countries.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Inquiries whether tobacco in all forms may be shipped to neutrals without question of ultimate destination.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Confirms report that tobacco and its extracts may be shipped without interference.

p.hi: Correspondence and Informal Arrangements Regarding the Importation of Goods from Germany and Occupied Territory Under the British and French Declaration of March 1, 1915, and the Orders and Decrees for its Enforcement
importation of goods bought or ordered before march 1, 1915

row.cell: From the Secretary of the National Association of Importers.
Transmits resolution petitioning the Department to obtain modification of British embargo on dyestuffs, etc.
Appeal for protection against unlawful interference by Great Britain with trade in botanical medicinal drugs from Germany.
American importers must accept and pay for goods for which they have signed contracts with German manufacturers.
From the Commercial Adviser of the British Embassy to the Foreign Trade Adviser of the Department of State.
Gives assurance that contracts made before Mar. 1 will be dealt with leniently.
Resolutions asking Government to take steps to secure importation of non-contraband goods necessary to American industry.
From the Foreign Trade Adviser of the Department of State to the Commercial Adviser of the British Embassy.
Inquires British interpretation of term “American ownership.” Case of Mr. Wolf.
Printed circular of Foreign Trade Advisers of the Department of State.
Movement of American-owned goods in Germany. Importers advised to submit evidence of ownership and payment to the British Embassy.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Instructions to ascertain procedure of Oversea Trust in importation from Germany and Austria to America.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Method of procedure in exportation from Germany to the United States.
