Requests investigation of report that many boats equipped for destruction of submarines are being constructed in the United States for Great Britain.
Reply to note regarding exportation of arms and ammunition from the United States to the countries at war with Austria-Hungary and Germany.
It is reported that speed boats are being built in large numbers for the destruction of submarines.
Use to which speed boats are to be put is not known.
Transmits a letter from the managing editor of the Milwaukee Journal regarding an embargo on arms.
Inquires if motor-boats ready for shipment to Russia are to be used in the war.
To Diplomatic Officers in European Neutral Countries (telegram).
Instructions to obtain information regarding embargoes on arms and ammunition.
Motor-boats are for use of Russian Government in patrolling lakes and closed seas.
Collector of customs has been instructed to allow exportation of motor-boats.
Arms and ammunition embargoed and reasons therefor.
Italy has an embargo on arms and ammunition because they are needed at home.
Portugal has not embargoed arms and ammunition.
Sweden has embargoed arms and ammunition; reasons therefor.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Report on manufacture of arms and ammunition, and on embargo and reasons therefor.
No Spanish embargo on arms and ammunition but policy is to prevent exportation in order to maintain neutrality and conserve supplies.
An embargo has been placed on arms and ammunition in order to conserve them for home use.
Report on neutral countries which have placed an embargo on arms and ammunition, with their reasons.
Information concerning warlike nature of speed boats built by Greenport Basin and Construction Co.

Transmits a letter from the Austro-Hungarian Consul at Philadelphia to the Editor of the “A Hét” Publishing Co., requesting publication of a notice to Austro-Hungarians working in U. S. munitions factories.
Transmits Foreign Office note submitting list of cases as evidence of use of American ammunition by French.
Six submarine destroyers for British loaded aboard the Bohemian sailing from Boston. Requests investigation.
Facts relative to Austro-Hungarian subjects do not constitute a violation of Federal criminal laws.
Press reports indicate that submarines constructed in the United States have been sent to England. Inquires regarding line to be taken in meeting Austro-Hungarian criticism.
To the Electric Boat Co. The same to the Bethlehem Steel Corporation.
Inquiry regarding shipment to England of submarines delivered to Vickers-Maxim, Montreal.
Transmits further statement from Burian regarding traffic in arms and ammunition between the United States and the Allies, with comments.
From the President of the Electric Boat Co.
Reply to inquiry about shipment to England of submarines delivered to Vickers-Maxim, Montreal.
The motor-boats shipped on the Bohemian were not armed.
There is no evidence that submarines have been built in the United States for delivery during present war.
Cites cases of boats built in the United States for use of the Allies, as breaches of neutrality.
After investigation of specific cases cited, the charge of violation of neutrality is denied.

p.hi: Loans to Belligerent Governments

row.cell: Notice issued to the press by the Department of State.
Loans to belligerents disapproved by this Government, but no action has been taken.

div.p: Treatment of Belligerent Warships, Their Crews and Tenders, in American Ports—Internment of the “Farn” (“KD–3”), the “Prinz Eitel Friedrich,” and the “ Kronprinz Wilhelm”

row.cell: Requests detention of the Farn, former British vessel, captured by Germans and named the KD–3.
Requests protection of British ship Farn taken into port at San Juan.
Memorandum of the Counselor for the Department of State.
Explained orally to the German Ambassador the decision of this Government as to character of the Farn and treatment she would receive.
The KD–3 was interned and British officers and Chinese crew released.
Presents argument for release of the Farn.
Decision holds to intern the Farn as a fleet auxiliary until the end of the war. Reasons given.
Memorandum of the Counselor for the Department of State.
Conversation with the German Ambassador on the subject of internment of the Prinz Eitel Friedrich.
Requests time for repairs on the Prinz Eitel Friedrich.
From the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Transmits report of Collector of Customs at Newport News regarding the Prinz Eitel Friedrich, with copy of his letter to the commander.
Announces the length of time that the Prinz Eitel Friedrich will be permitted to remain in U. S. waters for repairs.
States that the Prinz Eitel Friedrich was not in need of repairs. Inquires what steps will be taken in the matter.
British Government inquires as to whom the United States will hand over the Farn at the end of the war.
Instruction has been given that the Prinz Eitel may not leave within 24 hours after departure of an enemy merchant ship.
From the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Transmits inquiry from the commander of the Prinz Eitel regarding time for sailing.
Repairs on the Prinz Eitel fall within the principles laid down by Hague Convention XIII.
The right to claim the Farn is a question to be decided by the British and German Governments.
To the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury (telegram).
Recommends that commander of the Prinz Eitel be informed of the departure of enemy merchant vessels, as requested.
From the Collector of Customs, Los Angeles, to the Secretary of the Treasury (telegram).
Requests instructions regarding the, British collier Lena, which desires to make repairs and take on excess supplies.
To the Secretary of the Treasury (telegram).
Instructions regarding the stay of the Lena in San Diego port.
From the Secretary of the Navy.
Forwards telegram from officer of the Wyoming announcing internment of the Prinz Eitel Friedrich.
Expresses gratitude for protection afforded the Prinz Eitel Friedrich.
Requests permission for the Kronprinz Wilhelm to land certain persons and procure repairs and supplies at Newport News.
Announces time limit for repairs on the Kronprinz Wilhelm, after which, if vessel does not leave, she will be interned.
Asserts that the Kronprinz Wilhelm was apparently damaged by ramming the Wilfred M.
From the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Forwards letter from commander of the Kronprinz Wilhelm saying he will intern.
Expresses thanks for treatment of the Kronprinz Wilhelm.
British reserve their rights in regard to release of the Farn.
Arrest of officers of the Prinz Eitel Friedrich who had escaped from the United States. Suggests precautions to prevent further escapes.
Reports that Halbrock had not been interned and that Max Kjier was discharged in South American port on account of sickness.
From the Secretary of the Navy.
Refusal to permit the officers of the Kronprinz Wilhelm to own pleasure yacht.
Asks for personal description of the officers of the Kronprinz Wilhelm who escaped on the Eclipse, in order to assist in their capture.
Requests permission to put the Kronprinz Wilhelm and the Prinz Eitel Friedrich in repair for passenger accommodation.
Calls attention to escape of officers and men who were interned in American ports.
Requests that officers and men on interned vessels be spared the humiliation of having their pictures taken as a means of preventing their escape.
No pictures will be taken of interned German officers. Other means will be employed to prevent their escape.
Communicates all facts available concerning escape of interned German officers and men.
Refuses permission for full repair to interned vessels and restoration for passenger accommodation.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits note from the Consul at Edinburg containing letter from Lieutenant Koch, who escaped from internment at Norfolk, asking permission to return to his vessel in the United States.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain.
No representations will be made for return to the United States of Lieutenant Koch.

p.hi: Treatment of Armed Merchant Ships

row.cell: Inquires as to regulations regarding the arming of vessels for defense against submarines.
No objection to steamships entering American port, if armed for defense only.
From the Counselor for the Department of State to the British Ambassador.
Requests removal of guns from merchant ship Asian in New Orleans port.
Inquires attitude of the United States toward armed merchant vessels. Extract from New York Times, July 28.
Reply regarding status of armed merchant vessels.
Requests removal of guns from the Waimana before leaving port of Norfolk.
British reluctant to compromise right of protecting merchantmen by armament. Proper measures will be taken to insure compliance with regulations.
British Government must give assurance that armament of the Waimana will be used only for defensive purposes; otherwise guns must be landed.
From the Collector of Customs, Norfolk, to the Secretary of the Treasury.
Reports that Waimana cleared after coaling and landing a gun; tonnage tax collected under protest.

p.hi: Treatment of Merchant Ships Supplying Belligerent Warships—The Detention of the “Odenwald”—The “Pisa” Case

row.cell: Joint Resolution by the Senate and House of Representatives.
Customs regulations to empower the President to better enforce and maintain the neutrality of the United States.
U. S. Government responsible for supplying German warships from U. S. territory. Protests action of German vessels in American ports.
Discusses neutrality resolution and inquires as to its interpretation regarding use of territorial waters as base of operations for armed forces of belligerents.
Reexamination of German vessels in U. S. ports has been ordered.
From the Secretary of the Treasury.
The Odenwald has applied for clearance to Hamburg, carrying bunker coal. Have inquired whether any suspicious circumstances.
From the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Have instructed collector of customs at San Juan to search the Odenwald for arms and make report.
From the Secretary of the Treasury.
Quotes cablegrams from collector of customs, San Juan, giving assurance regarding the Odenwald.
Has been informed that the Odenwald will leave port for belligerent purposes.
From the Commanding Officer in Porto Rico to the Adjutant General at New York (telegram).
The Odenwald attempted to leave without clearance papers. Warning shot brought her back.
After reexamination of German vessels, this Government is satisfied regarding its duties as a neutral.
The Pisa will sail for Hamburg with coal and provisions and will try to communicate with a German cruiser at sea. Argument to prove this not contrary to U. S. regulations.
States that certain German steamships intend to leave U. S. ports to supply German warships and conduct belligerent operations.
Protests action of harbor authorities in firing on the Odenwald. Explanation desired as to why clearance papers were denied.
From the German Ambassador to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Official explanation desired as to why clearance papers were denied the Pisa.
Presents argument sustaining the U. S. Government in withholding permission for the Pisa to leave port.
Breach of navigation laws by the Odenwald a justification of acts of harbor officials.
Requests postponement of trial of cases involving Hamburg-American Line pending discussion of law with respect to shipments from neutral territory of coal for belligerent vessels.
Refuses to interfere with procedure of Department of Justice in cases of the Hamburg-American Line.
Requests that questions involving military secrets of German Government be avoided in trial of the Pisa.
Neutral territory as a base for naval operations on the high seas and judicial investigation involving military or political secrets of a belligerent government.
Representations regarding prosecutions against the Hamburg-American Line and the violation of neutrality laws.

p.hi: Actions of Belligerent Warships Outside and Within Territorial Waters—Hovering

row.cell: Renewed orders to officers on duty in the North Atlantic regarding observance of U. S. neutrality laws.
Protests against belligerent ships receiving supplies in vicinity of California. Cites case of the Bellerophon.
Case of the Bellerophon will be brought to attention of the British Government.
From the British Ambassador to the Counselor for the Department of State.
Forwards reasons why it would be impracticable for British warships to provision themselves from U. S. territory.
Calls attention to British cruiser Suffolk communicating with shore off Cape Henry.
Cites cases similar to that of the Suffolk and asks what action was taken by the Government.
Categorical denial that Suffolk has communicated with the shore.
Explains operations in North Pacific of the British cruiser Rainbow.
From the Acting Secretary of the Navy.
Transmits copies of correspondence referring to action of the Iroquois (1861) in receiving information of the movements of the Sumter.
To the Secretary of the Navy.
Inquires whether the Navy Department approved of action of the Iroquois (1861) in arranging for shore signals regarding movements of the Sumter.
From the Secretary of the Navy.
Record of proceedings in case of the Iroquois (1861) is not on file in Navy Department.
Protests against British warship chasing Danish ship Vinland within American waters.
Facts in case of the Vinland are not as reported.
Protests against hovering of British warships about American coasts and ports.
Quotes Navy report of a British cruiser off Galveston Harbor outside of the three-mile limit.
Acknowledges receipt of note of protest against hovering of warships near American waters.
Calls attention to hovering of French cruiser Descartes off coast of San Juan.
Investigation will be made concerning the Descartes.

p.hi: Control Over Wireless Telegraphy—Establishment of a Censorship at the Guam Cable Station

row.cell: Inquires whether wireless stations in the United States are forbidden to receive or forward code messages from and to the nations at war.
Reply to inquiry regarding transmission of radio messages in code to and from belligerents.
Governor of British Honduras asks permission to send commercial messages by radio through New Orleans in code.
From the Counselor of the German Embassy to the Counselor for the Department of State
Requests information regarding sending of code messages through Tuckerton radio station.
From the Counselor for the Department of State to the Counselor of the German Embassy.
Wireless messages in code may be sent through Tuckerton on condition that key to code and plain messages are sent to Department.
Sends key to cipher to be used in messages through Tuckerton and Sayville.
From the Counselor for the Department of State to the German Ambassador.
Asks if Embassy objects to sending messages in English between Washington and Tuckerton, cipher to be used between Tuckerton and Berlin.
To the Secretary of the Navy.
German Embassy to send official messages to the Navy Department for transmittal via Tuckerton: code also to be sent.
Refuses permission to send commercial messages from British Honduras through New Orleans in code.
From the Secretary of the Navy.
Program of procedure to be used in handling code messages of German Embassy.
Radio station at Sayville is in hands of Germans. Requests the United States to prevent unneutral use.
From the Acting Secretary of of the Navy.
Transmits cablegram from commandant of naval station, Guam, relative to establishment of censorship over cables.
From the Acting Secretary of the Navy.
Forwards telegrams sent and received relative to censorship of the cable at Guam.
From the Acting Secretary of the Navy.
Forwards from the commandant of naval station at Guam copy of rules governing receipt and transmission of local cable messages.

p.hi: The Prevention of Activities in the United States for the Destruction of Belligerent Merchant Ships and Property

row.cell: Requests extradition of Vernil Horne accused of attempting to destroy bridge in New Brunswick: suggests that international bridges be guarded by the United States.
Local authorities have sole jurisdiction and responsibility in respect of bridges. Federal authorities act only when called upon.
Calls attention to conspiracies in America for destruction of British ships and railways.
Special guard has been provided in New York Harbor to prevent the placing of explosives on British vessels.
Offers to cooperate with the U. S. authorities in suppressing conspiracies.
Calls attention to German responsibility for incendiary fires discovered on British steamers leaving New York.
Agents of Federal Government are cooperating with New York police to prevent the placing of incendiary bombs on vessels leaving New York.
To the British Ambassador. The same, except first and fourth paragraphs, to the French Ambassador.
Official investigation of attempts to destroy the British steamship Asuncion de Larrinaga.

div.p: PART IV: OTHER PROBLEMS AND RESPONSIBILITIES

p.hi: New Regulations Regarding the Issuance and Control of Passports

row.cell: Requests that passports not be issued for travel into Belgium.
To the Ambassadors and Ministers in France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, and Denmark (telegram).
Instructions not to issue emergency passports for travel in Belgium except under specified conditions.
To American Diplomatic and Consular Officers (including Consular Agents).
Consular regulations: Termination, extension, and amendment of passports, and advice for Americans traveling abroad.
Inquiries if a person, previously denied passport, is entitled to return to the United States to resume citizenship.
Persons who have long resided abroad, trying to escape from war conditions should not have passports.
Rules governing the granting and issuing of passports to those who have declared their intention to become citizens of the United States.
Passports denied to applicants who intend to enlist in belligerent armies.
Approves course in hot issuing passports to American citizens intending to enlist in belligerent armies.
Instructions regarding the passport of Trumbull, of the Rockefeller Foundation.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram). The same to the Ambassador in Germany.
Instructions to take up passport of James Archibald and give him emergency passport for immediate return to the United States.
From the Minisister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Archibald expects to sail for New York Sept. 8.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Proposes that no emergency passports be issued after Dec. 1 except in extraordinary emergency.
Foreigners leaving the United States should be provided with passports of their government.
Rules governing the granting and issuing of passports in the United States.
To Diplomatic Representatives of Foreign Governments.

p.hi: Diplomatic Representation in Bulgaria

row.cell: To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Arranging for diplomatic representation in Bulgaria if relations are severed between that country and the Entente.
To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Awaiting approval of Bulgarian Government to send Einstein to Sofia as Chargé on special mission. He will assume charge of British interests.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Einstein appointed special agent to assist in caring for British interests in Bulgaria and not Chargé on special mission.
From the Special Agent in Bulgaria (telegram).
To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Einstein may Continue to enjoy individual rank of Chargé without holding office as such.

p.hi: Status of American Consular Officers in Belligerent Territory Occupied by Enemy Troops

row.cell: Transmits official notice of expiration of exequaturs of consuls in countries occupied by German Army.
German Government has canceled exequaturs; will create three consular posts. Belgium protests.
Right of German Government to suspend consular officers in conquered territory recognized.
Transmits Foreign Office note regarding Belgian protest against suspension of neutral consuls in Belgium.
Acknowledges note referring to German announcement of intention to cancel exequaturs of foreign consuls.
Transmits copy of second note of protest to Germany against cancellation of exequaturs of foreign consuls in Belgium.
Transmits Foreign Office note commending the U. S. consular officers at Antwerp and Liége and suggesting that the post at Brussels be filled.
Requests information regarding position of Consul Young, who desires to return to Belgrade.
Awaits instruction regarding status of Consul Young now within Austro-Hungarian lines.
Young to remain at Belgrade under Austro-Hungarian control, though detached from Budapest jurisdiction.
Austro-Hungarian Government consents to Young’s return to Belgrade under certain conditions. Suggestion that he be detailed to assist at Vienna.
Young is to seal archives in Belgrade and proceed to Vienna, where he has been assigned for temporary duty in the Consulate General.

p.hi: Request for the Recall of Diplomatic and Consular Officers of Belligerent Governments: Von Loehneysen, German Consul at Seattle; Dumba, Austro-Hungarian Ambassador; Von Papen and Boy-Ed, German Attachés

row.cell: Requests recall of the German Consul at Seattle. Encloses letter from the Consul to Private Krüger commanding him to desert from U. S. Army for military duty in Germany.
Explanation of conduct of the Consul at Seattle and request that proposal to recall him be dismissed.
Conduct of the German Consul at Seattle is a serious offense against laws of the United States. Repeats request for his recall.
Announces that the Consul at Seattle has been recalled.
Statement regarding criticisms of conduct of German representatives in the United States.
This Government desires to remove all causes of criticism of the German representatives.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Archibald, American war correspondent arrested by British on charge of performing unneutral service, freed upon confiscation of letters.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits copy of a despatch from Dumba to Burian, taken from Archibald, plotting strikes in American steel and munition factories.
Requests copy of his letter to Burian.
Dumba’s letter was sent in secret cipher; paraphrase only can be furnished.
The President requests the recall of Dumba, who is charged with conspiracy.
Request from Dumba, for transmission to his Government, for recall on leave of absence for personal report.
Requests safe-conduct for Dumba to report to his Government.
When Dumba is definitely recalled, safe-conduct will be requested of the British and French.
Burian reluctant to condemn Dumba without a hearing, but does not question genuineness of the letter.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits documents taken by British authorities from Archibald exposing the secret activities of Austro-Hungarian and German officials in the United States.
Repeats request for recall of Dumba as persona non grata.
Dumba refused safe-conduct for leave of absence. Department awaiting notice of his recall.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Kirk sent from Berlin with package from Department pouch containing vouchers and expense account for German propaganda in the United States and other countries. Awaiting instructions.
Arrangements made for safe return of Dumba; correspondence on subject.
British and French will permit safe passage of Dumba and party.
Transmits reply to note requesting recall of Dumba, in which wish is expressed for continued friendly relations between the two countries.
Interview with Burian arranging recall of Dumba.
Transmits Burian’s formal recall of Dumba.
Requests transmission of radiogram to Berlin regarding Lansing’s request for recall of Boy-Ed and Von Papen.
Formal statement that Boy-Ed and Von Papen are unacceptable to this Government.
Boy-Ed is desirous of discussing question of his recall with the Secretary of State.
His Government wishes to know why the recall of the attachés is requested.
Request for recall of Boy-Ed and Von Papen repeated. Names of others who have offended also mentioned.
Urges prompt compliance with request for recall of Boy-Ed and Von Papen.
Announces recall of naval and military attachés and requests that safe-conduct be obtained for them and their successors.
Safe-conduct has been requested for the attachés. When the acceptability of their successors has been decided safe-conducts will be provided for them.
Arrangements for return home of Boy-Ed and Von Papen.
Furnishes safe-conduct and passports for Boy-Ed and Von Papen.

p.hi: Protection of American Institutions and Interests in Turkey

row.cell: Transmits official notification of date of effect of the new regulations governing foreign institutions.
Proposes conference of presidents of American colleges to reach an understanding with Minister of Public Instruction as to changes in the new instructions.
Verbal consent of the Minister of War that the Tennessee and North Carolina may remain in Turkish waters.

Has succeeded in obtaining delay in enforcing regulations for foreign institutions. Requests data regarding status of foreign schools in the United States with view to obtaining reciprocity of treatment.
Detailed report regarding assistance rendered by American cruisers along Syrian coast to Americans and others wishing to leave Turkey.
American schools will open under great difficulties and restrictions.

p.hi: Special Efforts in Behalf of British, French, and Italian Nationals, and of Foreigners Generally, in Turkey

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Turkey (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Three Englishmen to be shot in retaliation for killing of Moslems in bombardment at Alexandretta. An indemnity to families might prevent the incident.
Communication between American, British, and Syrian authorities regarding the bombardment of Alexandretta.
Attack on Constantinople imminent. Have been asked to communicate with Allies with view to avoiding bombardment. Instructions desired.
Grants permission to act as an intermediary to save Constantinople from bombardment.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Turkey.
Transmits British expression of appreciation, to be conveyed to Morgenthau for his offer to pay indemnity to Moslem families. Negotiations left in his hands.
Grand Vizier disapproves threats of military commander. Discussion of indemnity for families of slain Moslems.
Constantinople fortifies against attack of the Allies. Suggests that Germany be informed of her responsibility for fate of non-Moslems.
Suggests that the Allies be requested to agree to neutral zone for protection of non-combatants.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). The same, mutatis mutandis, to the Ambassadors in France and Russia.
Morgenthau suggests establishment of neutral zones for safety of non-combatants.
To the Ambassador in Germany (telegram). The same, mutatis mutandis, to the Ambassador in Austria-Hungary.
Instructions to impress upon German Government the necessity of protection of non-combatants in case the Allies attack Constantinople.
Bombardment of Smyrna; truce; demands of Allies; probable resumption of hostilities.
Assurance given that Turkish Government will endeavor to protect non-combatants.
Satisfactory interview with Minister for Foreign Affairs regarding possible massacres in Turkey.
German Ambassador in Turkey has been instructed by his Government to use his influence for safety of non-combatants.
French Government cannot accept proposals of safety zones in Turkey.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British cannot accept proposals of safety zones in Turkey.
Russia declares that Constantinople will not be injured by the Allies unless Turks use it for military operations.
Agreement as to amount of indemnity for families of victims of British bombardment. English prisoners freed.
From the Consul General at Smyrna.
Transmits copy of his despatch to Morgenthau giving report of bombardment of Smyrna.
From the Ambassador in Turkey (telegram). Transmitted to the Ambassadors in Great Britain and France.
British and French subjects in Turkey will be sent to unfortified places to be exposed to Allied bombardment. Request that their Governments be notified.
English and French will be placed on Turkish transports as targets for Allied guns. Asks that this be brought to notice of Germany.
Instructions to notify German Government of Turkish intention to expose non-combatants to bombardment of the Allies.
Minister of War agreed to send only fifty non-combatants into the war zone, pending nature of reply from French and British Governments.
Twenty-six British and twenty-four French placed on board a transport for Gallipoli. Philip (Embassy Staff) accompanied them.
Department disapproves member of Embassy staff accompanying British and French on transport. Philip to return to Embassy.

Reported British attack on hospital and hospital ship in the Marmora. Turkey desires to carry on war in humane manner; has sent back non-combatants from Dardanelles after admonition of German and Austrian Ambassadors.
The fifty belligerents [non-combatants] were set free. Philip’s presence most useful. Most of Gallipoli’s population has departed.
Instructions to request the Tennessee to take on board at Beirut Italian consuls from Syria and those at Jerusalem and Haifa, landing them at Alexandria.
Deportation of belligerent subjects from Aleppo commenced.
New law empowers military to expel populations whenever they regard it necessary. Deportations of British and French from Damascus begun.
Negotiations for release of British and French subjects in Turkey since beginning of the war.
British Government has informed Department of danger from mines in blockaded area and suggests arrangement with the Turkish Government for embarkation of the Italian colony from Sighajik.
Italian, Russian and Montenegrin interests in Turkey. Arrangements being made for Italian subjects to leave Turkey.
From the Ambassador in Turkey (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassadors in Great Britain and France.
Turkish Government has frustrated plans to transport Italians. Asks that French and British be requested to arrange for transportation of Jews.
From the Ambassador in Turkey (telegram). Transmitted to the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Permission to distribute relief funds refused. Ill treatment of deported Armenians. Christians in danger. British Jews awaiting transportation.
British and French who are forced to leave Turkey may land at Crete.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Turkey.
Egyptian Government has agreed to give deported Jews refuge in Egypt. Morgenthau requested to make arrangements.
War Office has promised to send civil subjects of belligerents to Aintab.
Interned persons at Urfa being sent to Konia.

p.hi: Efforts in Behalf of Armenians and Jews in Turkey

row.cell: Sentiment in Syria and Palestine is against the Jews. Instructions to attempt to secure a Turkish order holding civil and military officials responsible for lives and property.
Minister of Interior states that Jews and Christians are safe. Have requested Sublime Porte to send instructions for their protection to Syria and Palestine.
Armenian Church appeals to the United States to prevent massacres.
American citizen of Persian origin arrested. Concerted movement against non-Turkish element.
Urge Turkish Government to protect Armenians and Zionists.
Joined by Italian Ambassador in making Strong representations to Sublime Porte for safety of innocent people. Movement against Zionists suspended.
From the Ambassador in France (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Turkey.
Transmits Foreign Office message for Ottoman Government, protesting massacre of Armenians and holding Sublime Porte responsible.
Grand Vizier resentful at attempted interference by foreign governments. Persecutions of Armenians increasing.
Describes Turkish plan to crush the Armenian race.
From the Secretary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (telegram).
Inhuman treatment of Armenians by the Turks.
Approves his urging Turkish officials to stop Armenian persecutions. Inquires if any American citizens have been injured.
To the Secretary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions.
Turkish Government claims that a large number of Armenians are in armed rebellion against Turkish authority.
The Embassy has not heard of any injury to American citizens in Turkey.
German Government objects to statements made by Turks that anti-Armenian measures originated with Germans.
Suggests that the United States appeal to both Turkey and Germany in an effort to stop persecution of Armenians.
Inquires if protest by German Ambassador has improved conditions.
Protestant and Catholic Armenians exempt from deportation. Have requested exemption of all connected with colleges and institutions.
German Ambassador’s protest has not improved conditions. Bulgarians have made strong representations.
Suggests that a committee be formed to raise funds for assisting in emigration of Armenians to west coast of America.
Insurmountable difficulties in way of wholesale emigration of Armenians. Inquires if money would relieve situation.
Instructions to continue good offices for amelioration of Armenian conditions. Persecution is destroying U. S. good will toward Turkey.
Asks permission for Armenians to leave Turkey if they have relatives in America who will pay their expenses.
Sublime Porte will consider applications for emigration of Armenians to the United States.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Netherland Minister at Constantinople instructed to join the U. S. Ambassador in efforts to prevent Armenian atrocities.
Transmits copy of German memorandum to Turkey regarding acts of violence against Armenians.

p.hi: Protection of Germans and Turks in Persia

row.cell: Instructions to act in behalf of Germans captured on Persian territory.
Statements of German authorities regarding treatment of Germans expelled from Persia, are without foundation.
German Ambassador requests Russia to liberate Germans taken prisoner on neutral territory.
Transmits Russian note stating grounds for declining to liberate the Germans arrested in Persia.
Instructions to inquire for the German Government whether Russia has freed German prisoners taken in Persia.
German families allowed refuge in the Embassy. Protection and use of our flag asked by the Turkish Ambassador.
From the Ambassador in Russia (telegram). Communicated to the German Ambassador.
Russia will not liberate German prisoners taken in Persia.
American flag may be used over Turkish Legation unless the Persian Government objects.
Asks on what grounds Russian Government refuses to free German prisoners.
Inquiry should be made of Persia as to grounds on which Germans were taken prisoner.
Russian army near Teheran; Turkish Ambassador and German Minister have fled. Have assumed charge of their Legations. Persian officials ask protection.
Approves his assuming temporary charge of German and Turkish interests.
Recommends that our protection and flag be withdrawn from Turkish Embassy and German Legation until in imminent danger.
Cannot approve of any nationals taking refuge in our Legation unless in imminent danger of their lives.
Transmits Persian expression of thanks for safekeeping of archives, and notes from British and Russian Ministers regarding German and Turkish interests in Persia.

p.hi: Activities of the United States in Regard to Prisoners of War and Interned Civilians: American General Plan for Inspection and Relief

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Transmits letter from Chandler P. Anderson and memorandum concerning treatment by belligerents of enemy aliens and prisoners of war, and American relief work.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British request to communicate to Germany protest against inhuman treatment of British prisoners. Money will be furnished for their relief.
Instructions to communicate British protest against inhuman treatment of British prisoners in German camps.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram). Repeated to the Ambassador in Germany.
This Government willing to inspect prisoners’ camps and distribute food. Suggests plan of operation.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British Government requests that U. S. officials visit German prison camps and supervise distribution of money and provisions for British prisoners.
Plan for relief of prisoners to be communicated to the German Government.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
This Government will undertake the relief of British prisoners in Germany.
The United States is willing to tender its good offices to Austria-Hungary in behalf of prisoners of war if requested to do so.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
The British Government accepts U. S. plan for the aid of prisoners.
British are eager to begin relief of prisoners. Preliminary sum to be supplied at once if it can be used advantageously.
No authorization needed for acceptance of money for British prisoners. German Government has not replied to relief proposal.
Release and relief of Russian and Austro-Hungarian prisoners. Approval of American plan.
Inquires whether Austria-Hungary wishes to make formal request of Russia for reciprocity in relief of prisoners.
Austro-Hungarian Government anxious to make immediate ararrangements with Russia for camp inspection.
Transmits German official acceptance of relief proposals for prisoners, with certain restrictions.
Austria-Hungary desires to make an agreement with Russia for the inspection of prison camps. Outline of plan.
From the President of the United States to the Emperor of Russia.
Offers services of the U. S. Government and Red Cross for relief of prisoners in Siberia.
Instructions to confirm details of plan for relief of prisoners.
Desires notice of specific acceptance by Great Britain, France, and Russia of proposals regarding prison relief.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Requests copy of British reply to German proposals regarding condition of war prisoners.
Report on the working out of prison relief plan, giving names of men who will inspect prison camps.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits British note advocating similar arrangements in Great Britain and Germany for distribution of supplies and visitation of detention camps.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Grey requests that Germany be assured of British acceptance of the German scheme for inspection of prison camps.
Acknowledges receipt of British acceptance of German scheme of camp inspection.
Transmits Russian note with regulations regarding visitation of prison camps and distribution of supplies, and states that copy has been sent to American Embassy at Vienna.
Suggests that American and Spanish Ambassadors meet in Switzerland to confer with prison authorities regarding prisoners’ exchanges, etc.
From the Ambassador in Russia to the President.
Description of visit to the Tsar and delivery of the President’s letter of Mar. 18 regarding prisoners.
From the Ambassador in Russia to the Chief Clerk of the Department of State.
Transmits autograph letter from the Tsar to the President and note from Sazonov regarding reciprocal treatment of prisoners in Russia and in Germany and Austria-Hungary.
The United States is ready to cooperate in relief of Russian prisoners upon approval of Spanish, German, and Austrian Governments.
A conference regarding prisoners could not properly be initiated by this Government.
Russian Government will request Spanish approval of American relief work among Russian prisoners in Germany and Austria-Hungary.
Spanish Government instructs its ambassadors to render all assistance possible to Americans in prison-relief work.
Russian Government has given consent that American Red Cross operate throughout Russia in the most convenient way.

p.hi: Negotiations Relating to the Work of Belgian Relief

row.cell: Assurances given by Von Bissing that imported foodstuffs will not be requisitioned in occupied Belgian territory.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
German civil commander of Limburg has exacted a tax on foodstuffs imported for the relief of civilians. Shipments have been ordered discontinued until tax is removed and money refunded.
Inquires if import tax is exacted on foodstuffs sent for the relief of Limburg Province.
Transmits copy of his note to Zimmermann asking that no requisitions of food in Belgium be made during relief campaign and that relief ships be protected; also copy of reply.
Tax removed in Limburg Province and money refunded. Investigation dropped.
To the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Instructions to confirm report that tax has been removed and money refunded in Limburg Province.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits message from Hoover regarding food situation in Belgium and proposed methods of relief.
German Government guarantees not to molest foodstuffs imported for civilian population.
Requests permission to present to Foreign Office, Hoover’s request for permission to deliver maize to Belgian civilians.
Grants permission to present to Foreign Office Hoover’s request to deliver maize to Belgium.
Visit of Hoover to Germany in the interests of Belgium.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Tax on foodstuffs to Limburg Province said to be mistake on part of German authorities. Encloses a note from Gerard.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Cooperation of the Netherlands in facilitating transportation of supplies to Belgium.
Foreign Office will permit shipment of maize to Rotterdam for distribution in Belgium.
Transmits note from German military authorities in Belgium regarding the requisition of foodstuffs.
Transmits letter from German military authorities in Belgium stating that cattle and their food are exempt from requisition when imported by the Comité National.
German assurance that foodstuffs imported for Givet, Fumay, and other specified regions, will be exempt from requisition.
Encloses note from German military authorities in Belgium announcing exemption of pharmaceutical supplies from requisition.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Suggests that United States protest against German refusal to give safe-conduct for ships of the Relief Commission en route to and from Rotterdam.
From the Minister in the Netherlands (telegram).
Germany will permit Relief Commission ships to pass through English Channel unmolested; cannot give safe-conduct through war zone.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Grey gives assurance to the Relief Commission that neither its flag nor its markings will be used by the British.
From the Minister in the Netherlands.
Transmits German memorandum regarding the safe-conduct of relief ships. Comments thereon.
Instructions to bring to attention of German Government that the Elfland, a relief ship, was attacked by a German aeroplane.
Foreign Office declares that attack on the Elfland was made by mistake; suggests that horizontal markings on ships be erected.
Forwards despatch from London, for communication to Foreign Office, concerning the torpedoing of the Relief Commission ship Harpalyce and German refusal to grant safe-conducts.
Transportation difficulties encountered by the Belgian Relief Commission and antagonism of German Minister at The Hague.
German Legation and submarines instructed to let Relief Commission ships pass under certain conditions.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Grey requests that statements made by survivors of the Harpalyce be brought to the attention of the United States.
Transmits correspondence regarding permission of German Government for safe-conduct for certain relief ships.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Transmits report of German investigation of sinking of the Harpalyce.
Governor General has given assurances that, this year’s crop in his district shall be reserved for use of the Belgian civil population.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
British, German, and Dutch Governments agree to the use by the Relief Commission of German interned ships. United States consent is requested.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Inquires if British Government has officially sanctioned the use of German interned ships.
From the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
Plan to use German interned ships abandoned on account of objections of France.

p.hi: Negotiations Relating to the Work of the Red Cross

row.cell: Relation of Foreign Service officers to the Red Cross defined.
To the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Dr. Strong to be sent [to Servia] with large stores and hospital supplies.
From the Minister in Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria (telegram).
Transmits note from the Servian Minister of Foreign Affairs expressing gratitude for the relief of their sick and wounded.
Diplomatic and consular officers in Turkey will be allowed to serve as officers of the American Red Cross.
From the Chairman of the National Relief Board of the American Red Cross.
The Red Cross will recall the units of surgeons and nurses in Europe because of exhausted funds. It will continue to send hospital supplies.
To the Ambassadors and Ministers in European Belligerent Countries (telegram).
The Red Cross regrets the necessity of recalling its units of surgeons and nurses from belligerent countries.
German Government anxious to know if the American Red Cross will aid German and Austro-Hungarian prisoners in Russia and Siberia, expenses to be paid by Germany.
Application for permission for Red Cross to work among German prisoners in Russia calls forth an inquiry as to whether Russian prisoners will receive similar treatment in Germany
Red Cross to finance Russian mission in Germany to extent of $10,000. German Government will finance mission in Russia.
Foreign Office proposes that work of Red Cross be confined to visiting internment camps, distributing assistance, and studying Russian methods
Red Cross has proffered services to German prisoners in Russia. Inquires if like services to Russians in Germany are acceptable.
American Red Cross can be allowed only to distribute material aid to prisoners in Russia. Russia will not subscribe funds for support of Red Cross in Germany.
To the Ambassador in Great Britain (telegram).
American Red Cross has asked permits to send supplies to hospitals of Central powers, but without reply.
Instructions to ascertain exact attitude of Russian Government toward Red Cross and if withdrawal of units is desired. Forwards memorandum of the Russian Embassy.
British Government will pass medical stores to Germany if each shipment is guaranteed exclusive use by the Red Cross.
Further explanation of situation in Russia regarding Red Cross work.
Transmits statement to press that Great Britain has not refused shipment of hospital supplies to Central powers.

p.hi: Exemption of Hospital Supplies from Seizure as Contraband of War

row.cell: From the Ambassador in Great Britain.
Proposed list of hospital supplies would be accepted by Great Britain as non-contraband if accepted by other belligerents.
To the Ambassador in Italy. The same, mutatis mutandis, to the Ambassadors in France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Japan, Turkey, and Spain.
Instructions for joint action with Spanish representative regarding hospital supplies as non-contraband.
Asks to be informed of views prompting recent instructions to diplomatic representatives on subject of hospital supplies.
The United States could not withdraw from its expressed willingness to be of assistance when opportunity arrived.
Spanish Government has instructed its representatives to proceed jointly with the U. S. representatives in negotiations for exportation of hospital supplies.
Italian Government will consider as non-contraband medicines, sanitary supplies and surgical appliances.
Forwards German note to the Spanish Ambassador showing willingness to consider hospital supplies as non-contraband of war on basis of reciprocity.

p.hi: The Display of Distinguishing Marks by American Naval Vessels on the High Seas

row.cell: German Government requests that American warships in the Mediterranean display the national flag clearly by day and by night.
Transmits note from the Secretary of the Navy stating reasons why Navy Department must decline to issue orders as suggested by German Government.
From the Secretary of the Navy.
Department is unable to change its attitude in relation to the matter of display of flag.
Transmits note from Von Jagow stating that request to make flag clearly visible on American ships was a friendly suggestion, not an instruction.
